new.title: Stand before the Shrine of the Three Kings
new.desc: Behind the high altar of the Dom sits the golden reliquary said to hold the bones of the Magi, begun by the goldsmith Nicholas of Verdun in 1180. It is the reason the cathedral was built on this scale in the first place.
new.tip: Look out for the Gero Cross near the sacristy too: carved around 960, it is the oldest large crucifix north of the Alps.

new.title: Catch the light in the Richter window
new.desc: Since 2007 the south transept of the Dom has glowed with Gerhard Richter's window: about 11,500 squares of coloured glass, their order chosen at random by computer. Old and new Cologne in one wall of light.
new.tip: Come on a sunny morning or early afternoon, when the coloured pixels spill across the stone floor.

new.title: Climb the 533 steps of the Dom's south tower
new.desc: A narrow spiral staircase takes you about 100 metres up, past the giant bell Decke Pitter, to a viewing platform over the Rhine and the rooftops of the Altstadt.
new.tip: The last stretch is an open metal staircase, so skip it if you mind heights; reward yourself afterwards with cake and a Dom view at Café Reichard.

new.title: Walk across the love-lock bridge
new.desc: Since 2008 couples have clipped padlocks to the Hohenzollernbrücke, and by now hundreds of thousands hang there while more than 1,200 trains a day rumble past. Four Prussian kings on horseback guard the ramps.
new.tip: Cross from the Dom side to Deutz and sit on the wide steps by the river: that is the postcard view of the cathedral and the bridge.

new.title: Look up at Groß St. Martin from the Fischmarkt
new.desc: Its square tower with four turrets has crowned the Altstadt skyline since the 12th century, and it is one of the twelve great Romanesque churches of Cologne. Wrecked in 1942 to 1945, it was rebuilt stone by stone and only reopened in 1985.
new.tip: Stand on the riverside Fischmarkt among the colourful narrow houses for the classic angle on the clover-leaf choir.

new.title: Rub Tünnes's nose for luck
new.desc: The bronze duo Tünnes and Schäl are Cologne's favourite joke characters: the good-natured country lad and the sly city schemer from the Hänneschen puppet theatre. Tünnes's nose is polished to a shine by visitors chasing good luck.
new.tip: They stand just in front of Groß St. Martin; ask any local for a Tünnes-und-Schäl joke and you will get three.

new.title: Spot the Kallendresser on the Alter Markt
new.desc: High on a house front on the Alter Markt crouches a copper figure baring its behind over the gutter, a cheeky medieval motif recast by Ewald Mataré in 1957. Locals read it as Cologne's verdict on authority.
new.tip: Stand with your back to the Rathaus and look up at the gables on the opposite side of the square.

new.title: Hear the tale at the Heinzelmännchen fountain
new.desc: Legend says little house elves once did all of Cologne's work at night, until a tailor's curious wife scattered peas to trip them up and they vanished for good. This 1900 fountain tells the story step by step.
new.tip: It stands right opposite Brauhaus Früh am Dom, so read the tale here, then go and do some of your own work on a Kölsch.

new.title: Enter the Golden Chamber of St. Ursula
new.desc: In a side chamber of this Romanesque church, the walls up to the vault are covered in patterns made from human bones, said to be Ursula's companions, with rows of reliquary busts below. It is often called the largest bone mosaic anywhere.
new.tip: The chamber is usually opened only at set times or on request, so check with the parish before you go.

new.title: Stand under the dome of St. Gereon
new.desc: This church grew around a late Roman oval hall, and in the 1220s it was raised into a ten-sided domed space nearly 35 metres high, unique in the medieval West. The red and gold painted vault feels almost Byzantine.
new.tip: Go down to the crypt to find the 12th-century floor mosaic with scenes of David and Samson.

new.title: See Pop Art at Museum Ludwig
new.desc: Next to the Dom, Museum Ludwig holds one of Europe's best Pop Art collections, a huge Picasso holding, German Expressionism and photography. The zigzag roofline is a landmark of its own.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk through the Heinrich-Böll-Platz to the Rhine; the square is closed to footsteps during Philharmonie concerts below.

new.title: Find the quiet of Kolumba
new.desc: The archdiocese's art museum is built by Peter Zumthor right over the war ruins of the St. Kolumba church, mixing medieval treasures with contemporary art. Walking over the excavations in filtered light is the experience.
new.tip: There are hardly any labels: pick up the small booklet at the entrance and let the rooms speak.

new.title: Read the cell walls at the EL-DE-Haus
new.desc: The NS-Dokumentationszentrum is housed in the former Gestapo headquarters on Appellhofplatz. In the basement prison, the graffiti scratched by prisoners on the walls still survives.
new.tip: Allow at least two hours; the permanent exhibition upstairs on Cologne under National Socialism is as strong as the cells.

new.title: Take in the Dom from the KölnTriangle
new.desc: The 103-metre KölnTriangle in Deutz has an open viewing deck on its roof, looking straight across the Rhine at the cathedral and the Hohenzollern bridge. Many locals say it is the best Dom view of all.
new.tip: Go near sunset, when the cathedral turns golden and the trains on the bridge light up.

new.title: Walk under the Kranhäuser in the Rheinauhafen
new.desc: Three upside-down L-shaped towers stand on the old harbour quay, a modern echo of the cranes that once loaded ships here. The cobbled harbour promenade around them is one of the nicest Rhine walks in town.
new.tip: Start at the Chocolate Museum and walk south past the old swing bridge to the Kranhäuser and on to the Südbrücke.

new.title: Smell the first Eau de Cologne at Farina
new.desc: In 1709 Johann Maria Farina created the original Eau de Cologne in this house opposite the Rathaus, now called the oldest perfume house in the world. A guided tour takes you through its fragrance museum.
new.tip: Book a tour online ahead; they run in several languages, including English.

new.title: Laugh along at the Hänneschen-Theater
new.desc: Since 1802 Cologne's puppet theatre has staged the life of the made-up village of Knollendorf, with Hänneschen, Bärbelchen, Tünnes and Schäl all speaking Kölsch. It is a living piece of city identity, not just for kids.
new.tip: During Karneval the Puppensitzung parodies the city's carnival sessions; tickets go fast.

new.title: Dip a wafer in the Schokoladenmuseum fountain
new.desc: The ship-shaped Chocolate Museum on the tip of the Rheinauhafen shows how cocoa becomes chocolate, with a working production line and a three-metre chocolate fountain.
new.tip: Go early on a weekday; weekend afternoons are packed with families.

new.title: Shout Kölle Alaaf at 11:11 on 11 November
new.desc: Cologne's 'fifth season' starts every year at 11:11 on 11.11, when the Altstadt squares fill with costumed Jecken, brass bands and the new Dreigestirn. Carnival then pauses for Advent and returns in January.
new.tip: Arrive in costume well before 11; the Heumarkt fills up and access gets closed once it is full.

new.title: Skate at Heinzels Wintermärchen
new.desc: The Altstadt Christmas market on Alter Markt and Heumarkt is themed on the Heinzelmännchen elves, with more than 100 stalls and an ice rink that loops around the equestrian statue on the Heumarkt.
new.tip: The Heumarkt rink stays open into January, after the Christmas stalls have gone; groups can book an Eisstock lane.

new.title: Watch the Kölner Lichter over the Rhine
new.desc: One summer night a year, more than 60 boats sail in convoy down the Rhine while fireworks synchronised to music burst between the Zoobrücke and the Hohenzollernbrücke.
new.tip: Stake out a spot on the riverbank in the afternoon; there is free music on stages before dark.

new.title: Let a Köbes keep the Kölsch coming at Früh
new.desc: Früh am Dom is the classic Brauhaus in the cathedral's shadow: blue-aproned Köbes waiters carry Kölsch in a Kranz and swap your empty 0.2 litre Stange for a full one without asking. Each beer earns a pencil stroke on your coaster.
new.tip: To stop the refills, put your beer mat on top of your glass; leave the coaster with the strokes where the Köbes can see it at the end.
new.q: Früh am Dom, Am Hof 12, Köln

new.title: Drink Kölsch straight from the cellar at Päffgen
new.desc: On Friesenstraße, the Päffgen family still brews its own Kölsch in the house and serves it from wooden barrels in rooms with names like 'Beichtstuhl' (confessional). Plain, honest Rhineland cooking comes with it.
new.tip: Päffgen Kölsch is only poured in the family's own pubs, so this is the place to try it.

new.title: Order a Halve Hahn at Brauhaus Sion
new.desc: Ask for a 'half chicken' in Cologne and you get a rye roll with a thick slab of aged Gouda and mustard. Sion, near the Rathaus, has served drinks on this spot since the Middle Ages and does the snack right.
new.tip: Spread the mustard thickly, Cologne style, and wash it down with a fresh Sion Kölsch from the barrel.

new.title: Eat Himmel un Ääd at Peters Brauhaus
new.desc: 'Heaven and earth' is mashed potato and apple served with fried black pudding, the most Cologne dish there is. Peters serves it under coloured glass skylights in a house where beer was poured as early as 1544.
new.tip: Ask to sit in one of the small named rooms, such as the Kapellchen or the Malerwinkel.

new.title: Try Rhineland Sauerbraten at the Malzmühle
new.desc: The family-run Brauerei zur Malzmühle on the Heumarkt brews the soft Mühlen Kölsch and is known for its sweet and sour Rheinischer Sauerbraten with raisin gravy.
new.tip: Out of Kölsch mood? They also pour Koch's malt beer, a low-alcohol local classic.

new.title: Get a Kotelett at Lommerzheim in Deutz
new.desc: 'Lommi' is a cult corner pub on the Schäl Sick (the 'wrong' bank) with worn wood, no frills and enormous pork chops, a true Brauhaus experience away from the tourist crowds.
new.tip: It is tiny and popular, so reserve or come early, and expect old-school ways.

new.title: Queue for Adenauerbrot at Bäckerei Balkhausen
new.desc: This bakery on Apostelnstraße still bakes the Adenauerbrot, a bread with a high share of maize flour that Konrad Adenauer, then Cologne's mayor, devised during the First World War food shortages.
new.tip: Come in the morning; there is often a line out of the door later.

new.title: Have Baumkuchen at Café Wahlen
new.desc: Since 1911 this old-school Konditorei on the Ring has made its own pralines, cakes and layered Baumkuchen. The interior feels unchanged for decades, which is exactly the point.
new.tip: Take a box of pralines home; they make a better souvenir than anything on the Hohe Straße.

new.title: Bowl a round at Brauhaus Reissdorf
new.desc: The Reissdorf brewery was founded in the Severinsviertel in 1894, and its Brauhaus on Kleiner Griechenmarkt has a beer garden and its own automatic bowling alley in the house.
new.tip: Book the Kegelbahn ahead for a group night; on 1. FC Köln match days the games are shown with sound.

new.title: Wander among the graves of Melaten
new.desc: Cologne's grand cemetery lies on the grounds of a medieval leper hospital, with tree-lined avenues, the Millowitsch family grave and a famous Grim Reaper statue holding scythe and hourglass.
new.tip: Enter from Aachener Straße and look for the Sensenmann on the main avenue; the Tünnes figure on the Winters grave is a fun find too.

new.title: See the glass dome of the Central Mosque
new.desc: Opened in 2018 on Venloer Straße, the Zentralmoschee in Ehrenfeld wraps its prayer hall in curved concrete shells and glass, with two slender minarets. It has become a new landmark of the multicultural Veedel.
new.tip: Visitors are welcome outside prayer times; dress modestly and check for guided tours.

new.title: Find the lighthouse in landlocked Ehrenfeld
new.desc: Ehrenfeld's landmark is a lighthouse far from any sea, built in 1885 for the electrical firm Helios to show off its lamps. It never guided a ship, but it still shines over the Veedel.
new.tip: Combine it with the street art on Heliosstraße and Lichtstraße right around the corner.

new.title: Get lost in the Flora greenhouses
new.desc: The botanical garden next to the zoo has free show greenhouses with tropical and desert plants, more than 6,000 species and a raised walkway through the canopy. Cologne's oldest tree grows here too.
new.tip: Ride the Rhine cable car one way to make a half day of Flora, Zoo and Rheinpark.

new.title: Smell the roses on Fort X
new.desc: An old Prussian fort in Neustadt-Nord was turned into a 'green fort' in the 1920s, with a symmetrical rose garden on its rampart pushed by rose lover Konrad Adenauer. More than 70 varieties bloom here.
new.tip: Visit in June for the first big bloom and bring a book; the brick walls make it feel like a secret garden.

new.title: Walk the rhododendron gorge in the Forstbotanischer Garten
new.desc: In Rodenkirchen, this free tree garden holds thousands of woody plant species, a Japanese garden, roaming peacocks and a rhododendron gorge built into an old fortress ditch. The Friedenswald next door has trees from every country.
new.tip: Come in May when the rhododendrons are in full colour.

new.title: Find the 'Kapellchen' in old Rodenkirchen
new.desc: Rodenkirchen's old village core by the Rhine hides half-timbered houses, the old ferry house and Alt St. Maternus, a tiny church locals call 'Kapellchen'. It feels like a village, not a city.
new.tip: Walk on along the riverbank to the sandy beach a few minutes south.

new.title: Pass through the Severinstorburg into the Vringsveedel
new.desc: For centuries everyone coming to Cologne from the south had to pass this medieval gate on the Chlodwigplatz. Behind it, the long Severinstraße is the heart of the Südstadt with its Kneipen, cafés and old butchers.
new.tip: Walk the whole Severinstraße to St. Severin; there is an organic market on the church square on Tuesdays and Fridays.

new.title: End a Mülheim walk at St. Clemens
new.desc: Right on the Mülheimer Ufer, the little church of St. Clemens with its statue of St. Nepomuk gives this right-bank Veedel a quiet village feel, with wide views over the Rhine.
new.tip: Start at the Mülheimer Hafen and walk past the street art and Keupstraße before ending here at sunset.

new.title: Cross the steep Katzenbuckel bridge
new.desc: Built for the 1955 Bundesgartenschau, this sharply arched footbridge over the Mülheimer Hafen is a climb in itself and a lookout over the river and the city.
new.tip: On the other side, stroll through the Jugendpark and into the Rheinpark for a Dom view.

new.title: Stroll the Skulpturenpark by the Zoobrücke
new.desc: Between the Rhine and Riehler Straße, a small free park shows changing contemporary sculptures in the grass, a calm contrast to the busy zoo across the road.
new.tip: It is right by the cable car station, so stop in on your way to or from a gondola ride.

new.title: Find calm at the Museum of East Asian Art
new.desc: By the Aachener Weiher, Germany's oldest museum dedicated to East Asian art shows Chinese, Japanese and Korean works in a modern building with a Japanese garden courtyard.
new.tip: Afterwards, cross the road to the Aachener Weiher for a Kölsch in the beer garden.
new.q: Museum für Ostasiatische Kunst, Universitätsstraße 100, Köln

new.title: Hunt murals on an Ehrenfeld street-art walk
new.desc: Ehrenfeld packs more murals into a few streets than anywhere else in Cologne. Huge walls cover Heliosstraße, Lichtstraße, Körnerstraße and the railway embankment.
new.tip: Start at Heliosstraße 37 and zigzag to Körnerstraße, which has its own cafés and Cologne-themed fashion shops.

new.title: Float over the Rhine in the cable car
new.desc: Since 1957 the Kölner Seilbahn has carried little gondolas from Riehl, by the zoo, across the river to the Rheinpark in Deutz, with the Dom on the horizon.
new.tip: It runs only in the warmer months; kids can ride in a police-themed gondola.

new.title: Watch the sunset with the sheep on the Poller Wiesen
new.desc: Opposite the Rheinauhafen, the Poller Wiesen are wide meadows on the right bank where sheep graze, families barbecue and locals play football with the skyline in view. In autumn the sky fills with kites.
new.tip: Bring a blanket and something for the grill; the light on the Kranhäuser at sunset is the reward.

new.title: Rummage at the Nippes flea market
new.desc: On Sundays the Wilhelmplatz in Nippes fills with about 150 stalls of antiques, clothes and household things; new goods are not allowed, so everything has a past.
new.tip: Grab a coffee at the KaffeeKiosk and listen to the market haggling; the market runs on selected Sundays from spring to late autumn.

new.title: Have a drink among the iron giants of Odonien
new.desc: Sculptor Odo Rumpf turned a yard in Neuehrenfeld into his own 'country': an open-air studio full of huge metal sculptures that doubles as a venue for raves, art projects and a summer beer garden.
new.tip: Check the programme first; the Odonische Biergarten is the easiest way in on a warm evening.

new.title: Sweat in the Jugendstil Neptunbad
new.desc: Ehrenfeld's public baths opened in 1912 with glass domes and Villeroy & Boch tiles. Restored in 2002, the old pool hall is now a gym and the listed historic sauna sits beside a Japanese bathing area.
new.tip: Like most German saunas it is textile-free; bring a big towel to sit on.

new.title: Spend a summer evening at the Aachener Weiher
new.desc: The pond in the inner green belt is where Cologne goes on a warm evening: picnics, barbecues, sunbathing and a beer garden pouring cold Kölsch.
new.tip: Climb the short, steep Herkulesberg nearby for a view of the Dom spires over the Mediapark.

new.title: Feed the deer at the Lindenthaler Tierpark
new.desc: In the Stadtwald, a free little wildlife park lets you meet deer, donkeys, goats and sheep up close, a favourite Sunday outing for Cologne families.
new.tip: Bring coins for the feed dispensers instead of your own bread.

new.title: Swim in the Fühlinger See
new.desc: In Cologne's far north, a chain of lakes around a 2-kilometre rowing course is the city's summer swimming spot, and beautiful for a walk in winter too.
new.tip: Swim only in the marked bathing areas, as the regatta lanes are off limits.

new.title: Get a ticket for the Stunksitzung
new.desc: Since 1984 this alternative carnival show has mocked the stiff official Karneval sessions, the church and city politics. It has played in the E-Werk in Mülheim since 1991, for some 50 nights a season.
new.tip: Tickets sell out months ahead, so watch for the presale in autumn.

new.title: Catch Kamelle at the Rosenmontag parade
new.desc: On Rose Monday more than a million people line the streets as floats, bands and the Dreigestirn roll through the city, showering the crowd with sweets and flowers. The parade sets off from the Chlodwigplatz in the Südstadt.
new.tip: Bring a bag for the Kamelle and shout 'Kölle Alaaf'; the start in the Südstadt is livelier and less crushed than the Altstadt.

new.title: Lie on the sand at 'Köllefornia'
new.desc: Rodenkirchen's Rhine beach is a strip of fine sand where locals sunbathe, picnic and barbecue while barges glide past. Swimming is not advised because of the strong current.
new.tip: Paddling tours start nearby and drift downstream to the Zoobrücke if you want to get on the water safely.

new.title: Row a boat in the Volksgarten
new.desc: The Südstadt's park has a pond with rowing boats, ducks, table tennis and a big beer garden, a classic spot for Südstadt locals on a sunny afternoon.
new.tip: End at the Eierplätzchen nearby, an egg-shaped square with a kiosk where the Veedel meets for an evening drink.

new.title: Queue for charcoal skewers at Kebapland
new.desc: On Venloer Straße in Ehrenfeld, Kebapland grills skewers over charcoal and serves them in bread or on a plate. The line outside, late into the night, says it all.
new.tip: It is right by the Venloer Straße/Gürtel stop, perfect after a night at the clubs under the railway arches.

new.title: Eat falafel at Habibi in the Kwartier Latäng
new.desc: A student-quarter institution on Zülpicher Straße, Habibi serves falafel, shawarma and hummus for little money, with free cinnamon tea on the side.
new.tip: It stays open very late at weekends, which makes it the classic end to a night on Zülpicher Straße.

new.title: Order a schnitzel at Bei Oma Kleinmann
new.desc: A rustic Cologne Gaststätte in the student quarter, named after Paula Kleinmann, who cooked here into her late 80s. Locals come for the long schnitzel menu and the old-fashioned warmth.
new.tip: From October to December the kitchen also serves traditional goose; book ahead.
new.q: Bei Oma Kleinmann, Zülpicher Straße 9, Köln

new.title: Order Kölsche Kaviar at Brauhaus Pütz
new.desc: 'Cologne caviar' is no fish eggs but blood sausage with raw onions on a Röggelchen rye roll, a test for any newcomer. Pütz near Rudolfplatz pours Mühlen Kölsch to wash it down.
new.tip: Not feeling brave? Order a Halve Hahn and steal a bite from someone else's Kaviar.

new.title: Have a Kölsch on the Brüsseler Platz
new.desc: In the Belgisches Viertel, the square around St. Michael church becomes an open-air living room on summer evenings, with people sitting on the steps and Le Kiosk selling Kölsch, coffee and pastéis de nata.
new.tip: Start the evening at Hallmackenreuther, the café and bar on the same square, then roam the Belgian Quarter bars.

new.title: Lick a chocolate scoop at Eis-Engeln in Nippes
new.desc: A family ice cream parlour in Nippes since 1953, still trading under the old Konditorei Engeln sign. The chocolate ice cream is the neighbourhood favourite.
new.tip: Take your cone to the Schillplatz nearby and watch Nippes go by.

new.title: Brunch Turkish style at Petek Pastanesi in Kalk
new.desc: On Kalker Hauptstraße, Petek lays out an all-you-can-eat Turkish breakfast spread with endless tea, a cheap and generous welcome to the right bank.
new.tip: Leave room for the pastries from the counter and take some baklava home.

new.title: Eat grilled meat on Keupstraße
new.desc: Mülheim's Keupstraße is lined with Turkish and Kurdish bakeries, jewellers and grill restaurants. Mevlana is a favourite for grilled dishes.
new.tip: Walk the whole street before you choose; finish with tea and sweets at one of the pastry shops.

new.title: Eat Reibekuchen at the Sürther Bootshaus
new.desc: In quiet Sürth, the 'Côte da'Sürth' of Cologne, a boathouse terrace sits right on the Rhine. Mondays are for Reibekuchen, crispy potato fritters with apple sauce.
new.tip: Walk or cycle there along the river from Rodenkirchen; the Sürther Aue nature reserve lies just beyond.

new.title: Have a Kölsch with Rhine view at Brauhaus Quetsch
new.desc: On Rodenkirchen's main street, Brauhaus Quetsch has a beer garden looking out over the river and serves regional Brauhaus food.
new.tip: On Sundays try the Bergische Waffeln, waffles with cherries and cream from the hills east of Cologne.
